title: Procedural Programming
bullets: The idea that programs are made up of interconnected functions to manage and process data.

title: Procedural Programming
paragraphs: Procedural programming organizes a program around procedures or functions that perform specific tasks.

Basic structured programming focuses on clear control flow using sequence, selection, and repetition, while procedural programming adds stronger organization by dividing that logic into reusable functions.
The goal is to break a larger program into smaller procedures that can be understood and tested separately.

title: Focus on Functions
paragraphs: Procedural programming relies heavily on functions to organize a program into smaller sections of behaviour.
Each function usually receives data, performs a task, and may return a result.
Procedural programming simply uses functions as its main way of structuring program logic.

title: Using Functions for Input/Output Machines
paragraphs: A function can be thought of as a small input/output machine.
It receives values through parameters, processes those values, and can return a result.
This makes the function easier to reuse because the same logic can work with different inputs.
code:
def calculate_area(width, height):
    area = width * height
    return area

result = calculate_area(5, 3)
print(result)

title: Atomization
paragraphs: Atomization means breaking a larger program into smaller functions that each handle one part of the problem.
Instead of keeping all of the program's logic together, each major task becomes its own procedure.
This makes the program easier to read, test, and change.

examples.label: Without Functions
examples.code:
# Without Functions
name = input("Enter your name: ")
score1 = int(input("First score: "))
score2 = int(input("Second score: "))
average = (score1 + score2) / 2
print(f"{name}'s average is {average}.")
examples.expectedOutput:
Enter your name: Nathan
First score: 80
Second score: 90
Nathan's average is 85.0.

examples.label: With Functions
examples.expectedOutput:
Enter your name: Nathan
Enter a score: 80
Enter a score: 90
Nathan's average is 85.0.

title: One Function, One Task
paragraphs: A useful procedural programming guideline is that each function should have one clear responsibility.
Functions can contain several lines of code, but those lines should all contribute to the same task.
Separating unrelated jobs makes functions easier to understand, reuse, and test.

title: One Function, One Task
caption: Note: This example is an exaggeration. Keeping text to fit on a slide limits a function already to be kept pretty simple

examples.label: One Function, One Task
One Function Does Everything
examples.code:
# One Function Does Everything
def process_purchase():
    price = float(input("Item price: "))
    tax = price * 0.05
    total = price + tax
    print(f"Total: ${total:.2f}")
process_purchase()

title: One Bloated Mega Function
code:
import random


def play_battle():
    player_health = 100
    enemy_health = 80
    potions = 2
    score = 0

    print("A monster appears!")

    while player_health > 0 and enemy_health > 0:
        print("\n--- BATTLE STATUS ---")
        print(f"Player Health: {player_health}")
        print(f"Enemy Health: {enemy_health}")
        print(f"Potions: {potions}")
        print(f"Score: {score}")

        print("\nChoose an action:")
        print("1. Attack")
        print("2. Use Potion")

        choice = input("> ").strip()

        if choice == "1":
            damage = random.randint(10, 20)
            enemy_health -= damage
            score += damage

            print(f"You attack the monster for {damage} damage!")

            if enemy_health <= 0:
                enemy_health = 0
                print("You defeated the monster!")
                score += 100
                print(f"Final Score: {score}")
                break

        elif choice == "2":
            if potions > 0:
                healing = random.randint(20, 30)
                player_health += healing

                if player_health > 100:
                    player_health = 100

                potions -= 1

                print(f"You use a potion and recover {healing} health.")
            else:
                print("You do not have any potions left.")
                continue

        else:
            print("Invalid choice.")
            continue

        enemy_damage = random.randint(8, 18)
        player_health -= enemy_damage

        if player_health < 0:
            player_health = 0

        print(f"The monster attacks you for {enemy_damage} damage!")

        if player_health <= 0:
            print("You were defeated!")
            print(f"Final Score: {score}")
            break


play_battle()

title: Same Program Broken Into Smaller Functions
code:
import random


def display_status(player_health, enemy_health, potions, score):
    print("\n--- BATTLE STATUS ---")
    print(f"Player Health: {player_health}")
    print(f"Enemy Health: {enemy_health}")
    print(f"Potions: {potions}")
    print(f"Score: {score}")


def get_player_action():
    print("\nChoose an action:")
    print("1. Attack")
    print("2. Use Potion")

    return input("> ").strip()


def player_attack(enemy_health, score):
    damage = random.randint(10, 20)
    enemy_health -= damage
    score += damage

    if enemy_health < 0:
        enemy_health = 0

    print(f"You attack the monster for {damage} damage!")

    return enemy_health, score


def use_potion(player_health, potions):
    if potions <= 0:
        print("You do not have any potions left.")
        return player_health, potions, False

    healing = random.randint(20, 30)
    player_health += healing

    if player_health > 100:
        player_health = 100

    potions -= 1

    print(f"You use a potion and recover {healing} health.")

    return player_health, potions, True


def enemy_attack(player_health):
    damage = random.randint(8, 18)
    player_health -= damage

    if player_health < 0:
        player_health = 0

    print(f"The monster attacks you for {damage} damage!")

    return player_health


def display_game_over(player_health, score):
    if player_health > 0:
        print("You defeated the monster!")
        score += 100
    else:
        print("You were defeated!")

    print(f"Final Score: {score}")

    return score


def play_battle():
    player_health = 100
    enemy_health = 80
    potions = 2
    score = 0

    print("A monster appears!")

    while player_health > 0 and enemy_health > 0:
        display_status(player_health, enemy_health, potions, score)

        choice = get_player_action()

        if choice == "1":
            enemy_health, score = player_attack(enemy_health, score)

        elif choice == "2":
            player_health, potions, action_completed = use_potion(
                player_health,
                potions
            )

            if not action_completed:
                continue

        else:
            print("Invalid choice.")
            continue

        if enemy_health <= 0:
            break

        player_health = enemy_attack(player_health)

    display_game_over(player_health, score)


play_battle()

title: Stub Programming
paragraphs: Stub programming means creating the functions a program will need before writing their full behaviour.
A stub usually contains pass or a temporary placeholder so the overall structure of the program can be planned first.
This allows programmers to design how functions connect before completing each part.

title: Friendly Function Reminders – Type Hints
paragraphs: Always include type hints for your parameters and return values.
code:
def get_area(width: int, length: int) -> int:
    """Calculate the area of a rectangle.

    :param width: Width of the rectangle.
    :param length: Length of the rectangle
    :return: Area of the rectangle in units squared.
    """
    area = width * length
    return area

examples.label: Parameter type hints
examples.paragraph: Adding parameter type hints will help your code editor warn you when you are putting invalid input into a function.
examples.code:
def get_area(width: int, length: int) -> int:
    area = width * length
    return area

get_area("Hello", "World")

examples.label: Return type hints
examples.paragraph: Adding return type hints will help your code editor warn you when you are incorrectly using the return value.
examples.code:
def get_area(width: int, length: int) -> int:
    area = width * length
    return area

arbitrary_warning = len(get_area(3, 4))

title: Friendly Function Reminders – Docstrings
paragraphs: You should also always add correctly formatted docstrings.
code:
def get_area(width: int, length: int) -> int:
    """Calculate the area of a rectangle.

    :param width: Width of the rectangle.
    :param length: Length of the rectangle
    :return: Area of the rectangle in units squared.
    """
    area = width * length
    return area

title: Friendly Function Reminders – Docstrings
paragraphs: Docstrings will allow your code editor to explain your own code to you later, even when you don’t have it in front of you.
code:
def get_area(width: int, length: int) -> int:
    """Calculate the area of a rectangle.

    :param width: Width of the rectangle.
    :param length: Length of the rectangle
    :return: Area of the rectangle in units squared.
    """
    area = width * length
    return area

my_area = get_area(4, 8)

title: Wrap Up
bullets: Break programs into functions that each perform one clear task.
Use parameters for inputs and return values for results.
Use function stubs to plan and build a program in stages.
Make functions easier to understand with type hints and docstrings.
